title: std::string Essentials
summary: Create, measure, search, slice, edit, compare, and convert text with the most useful std::string methods.
intro: Names, emails, file names, and dates are all text. In C++ you hold text in `std::string`, a mutable string that manages its own memory. This lesson covers the methods you will use every day: measuring and joining, `find` and `substr`, editing in place, and converting to and from numbers.

steps.title: Creating, measuring, and joining
steps.body:
`std::string` from `<string>` holds text that can grow, shrink, and change. Create one from a literal, then ask it about itself.

```cpp
std::string s = "code";
s.size();    // 4, same as s.length()
s.empty();   // false
s[0];        // 'c', a char
s.front();   // 'c'
s.back();    // 'e'
```

Join text with `+`, which builds a new string, or `+=`, which appends to the end of an existing one. A `char` such as `'@'` joins too. `std::string(n, c)` builds a string of `n` copies of the char `c`, handy for underlines.

> Gotcha: a literal like `"a"` is a `const char` array, not a `std::string`, so `"a" + "b"` does not compile. Every `+` needs a `std::string` on at least one side. `first + " " + last` works because it runs left to right as `(first + " ") + last`.

In memory, a `std::string` object is 32 bytes here. Up to 15 chars fit inside the object itself, and longer text lives on the heap, which the string frees for you. Like `v[i]`, `s[i]` is not bounds-checked, and `front()` or `back()` on an empty string is undefined behavior, so check `empty()` first.

example.title: Name card
example.prompt: Build a full name with + and +=, measure it, read its first and last chars, and underline it.
example.output:
Grace Hopper
Length: 12
First: G
Last: r
Empty: false
============
example.explanation: `first + " "` works because `first` is a `std::string`, and `+=` then appends `last` to the same string. `Grace Hopper` has 12 chars, so `length()` is 12, `name[0]` is `G`, and `back()` is `r`. `std::string(name.size(), '=')` repeats `=` 12 times, so the underline matches the name exactly.

practice.title: Email card
practice.prompt:
Build an email address from two parts, measure it, and underline it.

1. Build `email` from `user`, the char `'@'`, and `domain` with `+`, then print it.
2. Print `Length: ` followed by its size.
3. Print `First: ` and `Last: ` followed by its first and last chars, each on its own line.
4. Print `Empty: ` followed by `empty()` as true or false.
5. Print a line of `-` exactly as long as the email with `std::string(n, c)`.

Expected output:

```text
ada@example.com
Length: 15
First: a
Last: m
Empty: false
---------------
```

tests.output:
ada@example.com
Length: 15
First: a
Last: m
Empty: false
---------------

hints: `user + '@' + domain` works because `user` is a `std::string`, so each `+` returns a new string.
`email.front()` and `email.back()` give the first and last chars.

steps.title: Searching and slicing
steps.body:
`s.find(x)` returns the index of the first match of a string or char, and `s.rfind(x)` the index of the last match. When there is no match, both return `std::string::npos`, the largest `std::size_t`.

```cpp
std::string s = "a-b-c";
std::size_t dash = s.find('-');        // 1
std::size_t next = s.find('-', dash + 1); // 3, search starts at 2
std::size_t last = s.rfind('-');       // 3
s.find("zz") == std::string::npos;     // true: not found
```

Store the result in `std::size_t` or `auto`, never in an `int`. `npos` is too big for an `int`, so it turns into -1 and mixes signed with unsigned math, which invites bugs.

`s.substr(pos, len)` copies `len` chars from `pos` into a new string, and `s.substr(pos)` copies to the end. Text between two positions `a` and `b` is `s.substr(a + 1, b - a - 1)`.

C++17 has no `starts_with`. Use `s.rfind(prefix, 0) == 0`: searching backward from position 0 can only match at the very start. For a suffix, check `s.size() >= suf.size() && s.substr(s.size() - suf.size()) == suf`.

> Gotcha: `substr` with a start past the end throws an exception and stops the program, but a length past the end just stops there. Only slice at positions you know are valid.

example.title: File name parts
example.prompt: Pull the year and extension out of a file name, then check for a word and a prefix.
example.output:
First _ at: 6
Second _ at: 11
Year: 2024
Extension: txt
Has draft: false
Starts with report: true
example.explanation: The first `_` is at index 6. Searching again from index 7 skips it and finds the second `_` at 11. The year starts right after the first `_` and is `11 - 6 - 1 = 4` chars long, so `substr(7, 4)` is `2024`. `rfind('.')` finds the last dot, and `substr(dot + 1)` runs to the end, giving `txt`. `find("draft")` misses and returns `npos`, so the check prints false, and `rfind("report", 0)` matches at index 0, so the prefix check prints true.

practice.title: Email parts
practice.prompt:
Pull the first name, last name, and top-level domain out of an email address.

1. Find the first `.` and print `Dot at: ` followed by its index.
2. Find `@` searching from just after that dot and print `@ at: ` followed by its index.
3. Print `First: ` followed by the text before the dot, then `Last: ` followed by the text between the dot and the `@`, each on its own line.
4. Find the last `.` with rfind and print `Domain: ` followed by everything after it.
5. With `std::cout << std::boolalpha`, print `Has army: ` followed by whether `army` appears, then `Starts with grace: ` followed by whether the email starts with `grace`.

Expected output:

```text
Dot at: 5
@ at: 12
First: grace
Last: hopper
Domain: mil
Has army: false
Starts with grace: true
```

tests.output:
Dot at: 5
@ at: 12
First: grace
Last: hopper
Domain: mil
Has army: false
Starts with grace: true

hints: Store each `find` result in a `const std::size_t`.
The first name is `email.substr(0, dot)`, and the last name has length `at - dot - 1`.
Compare `email.find("army")` with `std::string::npos`, and check the prefix with `email.rfind("grace", 0) == 0`.

steps.title: Editing in place
steps.body:
A `std::string` is mutable: these methods change the string in place instead of building a new one.

```cpp
std::string s = "cat";
s.insert(0, "a ");     // "a cat": insert text before index 0
s.replace(2, 3, "dog"); // "a dog": swap 3 chars at index 2 for "dog"
s.erase(0, 2);         // "dog": remove 2 chars starting at index 0
s.push_back('s');      // "dogs": append one char
s.pop_back();          // "dog": remove the last char
```

Positions often come from `find`, which returns the index of the first match, so you can edit text without counting by hand: `s.replace(s.find("cat"), 3, "dog")`. The replacement can be longer or shorter than what it replaces, and the rest of the string shifts to fit.

Each edit shifts everything after it, so find positions *after* the previous edit, not before. Inserting near the front of a long string moves every later char, which is fine for short text.

> Gotcha: `pop_back()` on an empty string is undefined behavior, and an `insert`, `erase`, or `replace` position past the end throws. Make sure the position came from a successful `find` before you use it.

example.title: Greeting edits
example.prompt: Edit a greeting in place with insert, replace, erase, and push_back, printing it after each edit.
example.output:
Hello World
Hello, big World
Hello, big C++
Hello, C++
Hello, C++!
example.explanation: `insert(5, ", big")` puts the text right after `Hello`. `find` then locates `World` at its new index, and `replace` swaps those 5 chars for the 3 chars `C++`, so the string shrinks. `erase` removes the 4 chars of `big ` at the index `find` reports, and `push_back` appends `!`. Every call changed the same `text` object, which is why it is not `const`.

practice.title: Date fixer
practice.prompt:
Turn `2024-1-5` into `2025-01-06` by editing the string in place.

1. Insert `0` at index 5 to make `2024-01-5`.
2. Insert `0` just after the last `-`, found with rfind, to make `2024-01-05`.
3. Replace the 4 chars at index 0 with `2025`.
4. Call pop_back, then push_back the char `'6'`.
5. Print `date` after each of the five edits, below the starting line the starter prints.

Expected output:

```text
2024-1-5
2024-01-5
2024-01-05
2025-01-05
2025-01-0
2025-01-06
```
hints: `date.insert(5, "0")` puts the new char before index 5.
After the first insert, `date.rfind('-') + 1` is the index of the day.
`date.replace(0, 4, "2025")` swaps the year, then `pop_back()` and `push_back('6')` change the last digit.

steps.title: Comparing and converting
steps.body:
`==` and `!=` compare the contents of two strings, char by char. `<` and `>` compare alphabetically by char code, and every uppercase letter comes before every lowercase one, so `"Zebra" < "apple"` is true. Digits compare as chars too, so the string `"10"` sorts before `"9"`.

```cpp
std::string a = "apple";
a == "apple";   // true: one side is a std::string
a < "banana";   // true
```

> Gotcha: with two bare literals, `"apple" < "banana"` compares memory addresses, not text. Keep at least one side a `std::string`.

Convert between text and numbers with functions from `<string>`:

```cpp
int n = std::stoi("42");        // 42
double d = std::stod("3.75");   // 3.75
std::string s = std::to_string(7); // "7"
```

`std::to_string` on a `double` always gives 6 decimals: `std::to_string(3.5)` is `"3.500000"`, and it ignores `std::setprecision`. When decimals matter, print the `double` itself with `std::fixed` and `std::setprecision`. `std::stoi("42abc")` stops at the first non-digit and gives 42, while text with no number at the start, like `"abc"`, throws, so only convert text you know is numeric for now.

example.title: Fruit and totals
example.prompt: Compare strings, parse numbers out of text, and turn numbers back into text.
example.output:
apple < banana: true
Zebra < apple: true
apple == Apple: false
Count: 50
Doubled: 7.5
Total: 50
3.500000
example.explanation: `a` comes before `b`, so `apple < banana` is true. `Z` is an uppercase letter, and uppercase sorts before lowercase, so `Zebra < apple` is true too. `apple == Apple` is false because `a` and `A` are different chars. `std::stoi("42")` gives the int 42, so `count` is 50, and `std::stod("3.75")` gives 3.75, doubled to 7.5. `std::to_string(count)` turns 50 into text so `+` can join it, and `std::to_string(3.5)` prints its fixed 6 decimals no matter what `setprecision` says.

practice.title: Usernames and years
practice.prompt:
Compare two usernames, parse two numbers, and build a label.

1. Print `alice == Alice: `, `alice < Alice: `, and `Alice < alice: ` each on its own line and followed by that comparison of `lower` and `upper`.
2. Parse `"1999"` with std::stoi into `year` and `"0.25"` with std::stod into `rate`.
3. Using `std::fixed << std::setprecision(1)`, print `Year: ` followed by `year` and `Times 4: ` followed by `rate * 4`.
4. Print the label `"Year " + std::to_string(year + 1)`.
5. Print `std::to_string(0.25)`.

Expected output:

```text
alice == Alice: false
alice < Alice: false
Alice < alice: true
Year: 1999
Times 4: 1.0
Year 2000
0.250000
```

tests.output:
alice == Alice: false
alice < Alice: false
Alice < alice: true
Year: 1999
Times 4: 1.0
Year 2000
0.250000

hints: Wrap each comparison in parentheses: `(lower == upper)`.
`A` sorts before `a`, so only `upper < lower` is true.

recap:
- `std::string` from `<string>` is mutable text: `size()` or `length()`, `empty()`, `s[i]`, `front()`, and `back()`.
- Join with `+` and `+=`, but never two bare literals. `std::string(n, c)` repeats a char.
- `find` and `rfind` return an index or `std::string::npos`, so store it in `std::size_t` or `auto`.
- `s.find(c, pos + 1)` finds the next match, and `substr(pos, len)` or `substr(pos)` copies a piece.
- C++17 has no `starts_with`: `s.rfind(prefix, 0) == 0` checks a prefix.
- `insert`, `erase`, `replace`, `push_back`, and `pop_back` edit the string in place.
- `==` compares contents, and `<` sorts by char code with uppercase first.
- `std::stoi` and `std::stod` parse text, `std::to_string` makes text, and on a `double` it always shows 6 decimals.
